lessons.title: Governance Plus Valuation: When a Clean Company Is Still a Bad Buy

body.text: Good governance tells you the numbers are real. It does not tell you the price is right. Honest management has never made an expensive stock cheap.

children.text: Everything in this course has been about avoiding a particular kind of loss: the one where the business was never what the accounts said, or where cash quietly left through a promoter's side door. That work protects you from permanent capital loss. It does not protect you from the other, more common way investors lose money, which is paying too much for something perfectly genuine. This final lesson puts the two together.

Rarely worth it; you are paying a premium price for a company with known governance gaps

body.text: Notice that only one box says buy without qualification. Most of the market, most of the time, sits in the other boxes. The purpose of this framework is not to find reasons to invest. It is to make you comfortable doing nothing until both axes line up.

children.text: The Arithmetic of Paying Too Much

Take a company that scores 38 on your checklist: honest, well run, strong returns on capital. You buy it at 60 times earnings, and it delivers exactly what you hoped, growing earnings 15% a year for five years. Earnings double, rising 2.01 times. Your return depends almost entirely on what multiple the market pays at the end.

body.title: Five-year annualised return, bought at 60 times earnings with 15% annual growth

children.text: The business did everything right. Governance was never in question. Yet at an exit multiple of 30, which is still a healthy multiple for most businesses, five years of 15% compounding produced roughly zero return. At 25 times, you lost money. This is how a genuinely good company becomes a bad investment, and no amount of governance work prevents it.

body.title: Where Does the Return Go?
body.prompt: You buy a well-governed company at 40 times earnings. Over five years its earnings grow 15% a year, so they rise 2.01 times, and the market rerates it down to 20 times earnings. By what factor does the share price change? Answer to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Price change = earnings growth × multiple change = 2.01 × (20 ÷ 40) = 1.01. Five years of excellent operating performance produced about 1% in total, because you handed back everything the business earned through the multiple. Multiple compression is the tax you pay for a high entry price, and it is charged whether or not management is honest.

body.text: In the Indian market, several well-governed consumer and quality names have traded above 60 or 70 times earnings at various points. Owning them through a period of multiple compression has produced years of flat returns for holders who paid those prices, even though earnings kept growing and no governance issue ever emerged. A high score is a reason to put a company on your list, not a licence to pay any price.

children.text: What Governance Analysis Cannot Tell You

columns.label: The Scorecard Answers
points: Is cash reaching all shareholders or leaking to insiders?
Is capital being reinvested at decent returns?
Does management keep its promises and respect disclosure rules?
How likely is a permanent, governance-driven loss?

columns.label: It Says Nothing About
points: Whether the industry is being disrupted
Whether current margins are at a cyclical peak
Whether competition is about to intensify
What the stock is worth today
Whether honest management can save a structurally declining business

children.text: There is no shortage of scrupulously honest managements running businesses that are slowly being competed out of existence. Governance analysis protects you from being cheated. It does not protect you from being wrong about the business, and the two failures feel identical in a portfolio statement.

A score is only useful if it changes what you do. The cleanest way to use it is to let the governance score decide position size and the valuation decide entry, rather than blending them into a single number that hides both.

body.caption: A simple way to link score, price, and position

cells: Your normal maximum for any single stock
A price you can justify on cash flows, not on the last five years of multiple expansion
Annual rescore, plus alerts on material events
About two thirds of your normal maximum
A visible discount to comparable, better-governed peers
Every quarter, focused on the items that scored 0
About one third, and only if you can name the catalyst
A large margin of safety on adjusted, not reported, earnings
Every quarter, with a pre-set exit trigger
Below 16
Zero
No price is low enough
Not applicable

body.text: One portfolio rule matters more than position size: do not hold several companies from the same promoter group. Governance risk is specific to people, so it is correlated across every company those people control. Three stocks from one group is one bet, not three, and Chapter 2 showed how quickly pressure in one group entity reaches the others.

children.text: Selling Rules, Written Before You Need Them

The hardest moment in governance investing is not the analysis. It is the morning a filing appears and the stock is down 15% before you have finished reading it. Lesson 11 showed how quickly liquidity disappears. Decide your triggers now, while nothing is happening, and write them next to each holding's scorecard.

cells: Auditor resigns citing missing information or unresolved concerns, or issues an adverse or disclaimer opinion
Exit, same day, without waiting for the company's explanation
Regulator restrains promoters or key executives from boards or the market
Exit
Related party loans, deposits, and guarantees cross 25% of net worth
Exit
Promoter pledge rises above half of promoter holding, or rises while the stock falls
Reduce sharply, and set a date to review the rest
Warrants or preferential shares issued to promoters at floor prices after a fall, with no clear funding need
Reduce, and vote against the resolution
Cash conversion falls for three consecutive years while profit grows
Rescore checks 12, 13, and 18 fully before doing anything else
Valuation runs far ahead of what cash flows justify, with governance unchanged
Trim, do not exit. This is a price problem, not a trust problem

children.text: Note the difference in the last two rows. Governance deterioration is a reason to sell whatever the price. Overvaluation is a reason to trim and wait, because the company is still worth owning at a different price. Confusing the two leads people to hold frauds because they look cheap, and to sell quality because it looks expensive.

body.title: Place the Stock
body.question: A company scores 36 on your checklist and trades at 72 times earnings, roughly double its own ten-year average multiple and well above better-priced peers. What is the correct action?
options: Buy, because a high governance score justifies any price for a quality business
Avoid buying now, add it to a watchlist with a price you would pay, and revisit when the multiple or your estimate of value changes
Avoid permanently, because a multiple this high always means the market is wrong
Buy a large position, since strong governance removes the risk of loss
body.explanation: Strong governance tells you the earnings are real and the business is likely to survive. It says nothing about whether 72 times those earnings is a sensible price. The company belongs on your list, with a price attached. Nothing about a high score removes the arithmetic of multiple compression.

body.title: The Last Decision of the Course
body.scenario: You have ₹5 lakh to invest and two candidates. Stock 1 is a consumer company scoring 37, with 25 years of consistent disclosure, no related party issues, and 18% ROCE, trading at 68 times earnings against a ten-year average of 45. Stock 2 is an industrial company scoring 27, trading at 14 times earnings, whose zeroes are on check 7 (two long-tenured independent directors also sitting on group boards) and check 19 (missed its stated margin target twice), with clean auditor reports, no related party loans, no pledge, and cash conversion above 0.8 for five years.
body.prompt: How would you allocate, and what would you write down today so your future self behaves consistently?
body.modelAnswer: Neither stock is disqualified, so this is a sizing and pricing decision rather than a trust decision. Stock 2 is investable now: a score of 27 is in the acceptable band, its two zeroes are governance-process weaknesses rather than cash leakage, and the things that matter most, auditor reports, related party exposure, pledge, and cash conversion, are all clean. Size it at about two thirds of your normal maximum and put the two zero items on a quarterly watch. Stock 1 is a better company at a worse price. At 68 times earnings against its own 45 times average, a large part of your future return depends on the multiple holding, which is not a business judgement you control. The sensible action is to set the price you would pay, perhaps closer to its long-run multiple, and wait, buying in tranches if it gets there. What to write down today: the maximum position for each, the specific events that would make you exit Stock 2 immediately, the price at which you would start buying Stock 1, and the date of the next rescore for both. Deciding this now, in writing, is what stops a falling price from looking like an opportunity and a rising price from looking like proof you were right.

body.title: Your Governance Investing Rules, in One Page
steps: Score every candidate on the 20 checks before you look at any valuation, so the price cannot influence the score
Apply the five red lines first; a red line ends the analysis regardless of price
Set the maximum position size from the score band, and the entry price from cash flows rather than recent multiples
Never hold more than one company from a promoter group whose governance you doubt
Write your exit triggers next to each holding on the day you buy it
Rescore annually, and immediately on an auditor change, a preferential issue, a regulatory action, or a jump in pledge
Keep every year's scorecard, because the direction of a company's governance matters more than its level at any one moment
Remember the division of labour: governance decides whether you can trust the numbers, valuation decides whether the numbers are worth the price

body.text: If you take one habit from this course, make it this: read the auditor's report and the related party note before you read the chairman's letter, on every company you own, every year. That single change in reading order would have kept investors out of most of the disasters covered in these six chapters.

This lesson is educational and is not investment advice. Position sizing, valuation thresholds, and exit rules are illustrative frameworks, not recommendations, and they should be adapted to your own circumstances and risk tolerance. Nothing here is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.

points: Governance tells you whether the numbers are real; valuation tells you whether they are worth the price, and you need both
Bought at 60 times earnings, a company growing profit 15% a year for five years returns about zero if the multiple falls to 30, and loses money at 25
The scorecard cannot tell you about disruption, cyclical peaks, competition, or what a business is worth today
Let the score set position size and the valuation set the entry price, rather than blending them into one number
Never treat several companies from one promoter group as separate holdings; governance risk follows people
Write exit triggers in advance: governance deterioration means sell at any price, while overvaluation means trim and wait
The habit that matters most is reading the auditor's report and the related party note before the chairman's letter, every year, on every company you own
